name: Sri Venkateswara Swamy Temple, Tirumala
summary: Hilltop temple of Lord Venkateswara on Venkatadri, one of the seven Seshachalam hills above Tirupati, and among the most visited pilgrimage shrines in the world. It is administered by Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams (TTD).
history: The shrine is praised in early Tamil Alvar hymns and is counted among the 108 Divya Desams. The earliest well-known endowment is dated to 966 CE, when the Pallava queen Samavai gifted jewels and land to fund festivals. The temple received support from the Cholas, Pandyas and local chiefs, and grew most in wealth and size under the Vijayanagara kings. Krishnadevaraya made major gifts in the early 16th century, including gold used to gild the Ananda Nilayam vimana over the sanctum, and his statue stands in the temple. Since 1933 the temple has been run by TTD.
significance: Devotees come for darshan of Venkateswara (Srinivasa, Balaji), offer hair as a vow (tonsure at Kalyana Katta) and take the laddu prasadam. The annual Brahmotsavam in September-October (Bhadrapada/Asvayuja) with its Garuda Seva and the Vaikuntha Ekadasi (December-January), when the Vaikuntha Dwaram is opened, draw the largest crowds. Daily rituals begin with Suprabhatam before dawn and end with Ekanta Seva at night.
built_period: Ancient; recorded endowments from the 10th century, expanded 14th-16th centuries (Vijayanagara)

name: Sri Padmavathi Ammavari Temple, Tiruchanoor
summary: Temple of Goddess Padmavathi (Alamelu Manga), consort of Lord Venkateswara, at Tiruchanoor about 5 km from Tirupati. Tradition holds that a visit to Tirumala is completed by darshan here.
history: Legend says the goddess emerged from a golden lotus in the temple tank, Padma Sarovaram, after the Lord performed penance here, which gave the place the name Alamelu Mangapuram. The temple is administered by Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams. Older shrines at the site include those of Krishna-Balarama and Sundararaja Swamy.
significance: Devotees seek the goddess's blessings for prosperity and family welfare, and many visit after Tirumala darshan. The main festival is the nine-day Karthika Brahmotsavam (November-December), which ends with Panchami Theertham, when the Sudarshana Chakra is dipped in Padma Sarovaram and thousands of devotees bathe in the tank. Kalyanotsavam and Friday rituals are also popular.

name: Sri Govindaraja Swamy Temple, Tirupati
address: Govindaraja Swamy Temple Street, near Tirupati railway station, Tirupati
summary: Large 12th-century temple in the heart of Tirupati town dedicated to Govindaraja, a reclining form of Vishnu, consecrated by Ramanujacharya. It is run by TTD.
history: Tradition holds that Ramanuja consecrated the temple in 1130 CE, and the settlement that grew around it became the town of Tirupati. Earlier the shrine is said to have centred on Parthasarathy, with Govindaraja later becoming the main deity. Inscriptions in the temple date from the 13th century, and it gained importance under the Saluva and Vijayanagara rulers in the early 16th century, when the tall eastern gopuram was raised.
significance: Devotees regard Govindaraja as the elder brother of Lord Venkateswara and visit the temple as part of the Tirupati circuit. The annual Brahmotsavam (around May-June) and the float festival (Teppotsavam) in the temple tank are the main events. The complex also contains shrines of Parthasarathy, Andal and the Alvars.

address: Kapila Theertham, foot of Tirumala hills, Tirupati
summary: Shiva temple at the foot of the Tirumala hills where a waterfall drops into the sacred Kapila Theertham tank. It is the main Shaiva shrine in Tirupati and is run by TTD.
history: Legend says the sage Kapila worshipped Shiva here and installed the lingam, which gives the temple its name. The lingam is housed at the mouth of a cave in the hillside. Inscriptions of the Chola period are reported at the site, and later additions are credited to the Vijayanagara period. The temple is administered by Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams.
significance: Devotees bathe in the tank fed by the hill waterfall, especially during the Karthika month and on Mukkoti (Kapila) Theertham day. Maha Shivaratri and the annual Brahmotsavam (around February) are the main festivals, along with Karthika Deepam and Vinayaka Chaturthi.

name: Sri Kalyana Venkateswara Swamy Temple, Srinivasa Mangapuram
summary: Temple of Lord Venkateswara at Srinivasa Mangapuram, about 12 km west of Tirupati, where tradition says the Lord stayed after his wedding with Padmavathi. It is maintained by TTD.
history: Legend holds that Venkateswara stayed here with Padmavathi after their marriage before going up to Tirumala. The present form of the temple is credited to Chinna Tirumalacharya, grandson of the poet-saint Annamacharya, in the 16th century. The temple is a protected monument of the Archaeological Survey of India and has been maintained by TTD since 1967, with regular utsavams revived from 1981.
significance: Newly married couples visit to seek the blessings of the Lord in his wedding form (Kalyana Venkateswara), and the daily Kalyanotsavam is popular with devotees unable to perform it at Tirumala. The annual Brahmotsavam (around February) is the main festival.

name: Sri Prasanna Venkateswara Swamy Temple, Appalayagunta
summary: TTD-run temple of Lord Venkateswara at Appalayagunta, about 15 km from Tirupati, where the deity is shown with the raised hand of blessing (abhaya hasta).
history: Tradition says that on his way to Tirumala after marrying Padmavathi, Venkateswara blessed the sage Siddheswara who was meditating here, and stayed in the abhaya pose at the sage's request. The temple is attributed to Venkata Perumalaraju Brahmadeva, a ruler of Karvetinagaram, and is dated in local accounts to 1232 CE. It has been managed by Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams since 1988.
significance: Unlike the main Tirumala idol, the deity here shows the abhaya hasta, and devotees come to seek relief and protection. A shrine of Anjaneya in the complex is visited by those seeking cure from chronic illness. The annual Brahmotsavam (around May-June) includes Dhwajarohanam, Kalyanotsavam, Garuda Seva, Rathotsavam and Chakrasnanam.

name: Sri Kalahasteeswara Swamy Temple, Srikalahasti
address: Srikalahasti, on the banks of the Swarnamukhi river
summary: Major Shiva temple at Srikalahasti, about 36 km from Tirupati, revered as the Vayu (air) linga among the five Pancha Bhoota Sthalams. It is widely known for the Rahu-Ketu dosha nivarana puja.
history: The name joins Sri (spider), Kala (serpent) and Hasti (elephant), three creatures said to have worshipped the linga here and won liberation; the hunter-devotee Kannappa is also linked to the shrine. The inner temple is ancient and was expanded by the Cholas in the 11th century. The Vijayanagara emperor Krishnadevaraya built the hundred-pillared mandapa and the large gopuram around 1516. The main rajagopuram collapsed in 2010 and was rebuilt.
significance: Shiva is worshipped as Kalahasteeswara with the goddess Gnana Prasunambika, and the lamp in the sanctum is said to flicker though there is no draught, which devotees link to the Vayu linga. Devotees perform the Rahu-Ketu puja to remove Rahu, Ketu and Kala Sarpa doshas, and the temple is unusual in staying open during eclipses. Maha Shivaratri Brahmotsavam (February-March) is the main festival.

name: Sri Varasiddhi Vinayaka Swamy Temple, Kanipakam
summary: Temple of the self-manifested (swayambhu) Ganesha at Kanipakam near Chittoor, where the idol sits in a well of water that never runs dry.
history: Tradition says three brothers who could not speak, hear or see were digging a well when their tool struck a stone that began to bleed; on touching the water they were cured, and the stone was revealed as Ganesha. The temple is attributed to the Chola king Kulothunga I in the early 11th century and was expanded under the Vijayanagara rulers in the 14th century. It is administered by the AP Endowments Department.
significance: Devotees believe the idol keeps growing and that the deity witnesses oaths, so disputes were traditionally settled by swearing before him. The 21-day Brahmotsavam beginning on Vinayaka Chavithi (August-September, Bhadrapada) is the main festival. Abhishekam with the theertham from the well is a principal ritual.

address: Srisailam, Nallamala hills, above the Krishna river
summary: Hilltop temple of Shiva as Mallikarjuna and the goddess Bhramaramba in the Nallamala forest, one of the twelve Jyotirlingas and one of the eighteen Maha Shakti Peethas.
history: Srisailam is praised in the Puranas and in the Tamil Tevaram hymns. Inscriptions record patronage from the Satavahanas onward, with major work by the Kakatiyas, the Reddi kings and the Vijayanagara rulers, who added mandapas and gopurams; Harihara Raya II built the mukha mandapa. Chhatrapati Shivaji built the northern gopuram in the 17th century. The temple is managed by the Srisaila Devasthanam under the AP Endowments Department.
significance: Devotees see it as unique in being both a Jyotirlinga and a Shakti Peetha. At Sparsha Darshan devotees may touch the linga. Maha Shivaratri Brahmotsavam (February-March), the Ugadi festival (March-April) when pilgrims from Karnataka and Maharashtra arrive on foot, and the Karthika month (October-November) are the busiest times.

name: Mahanandi (Sri Mahanandeeswara Swamy Temple)
summary: Shiva temple at the foot of the Nallamala hills about 15 km from Nandyal, known for its crystal-clear spring-fed pools and as the chief of the Nava Nandi shrines.
history: The original temple is attributed to the Badami Chalukyas around the 7th century, and inscriptions of the 10th century record repairs and rebuilding. The vimana over the sanctum follows the Chalukyan style, while later structures were added in the Vijayanagara period. One legend links the name to the worship of Nandi, while another tells of a cow that poured its milk on an anthill where the self-manifested linga was found.
significance: Devotees bathe in the Kalyani pools, whose water flows from a perennial spring said to rise beneath the linga and stays at a near-constant temperature. Mahanandi is the first of the Nava Nandis, nine Nandi shrines within about 15 km that pilgrims visit as a circuit. Maha Shivaratri (February-March) is the main festival.

name: Ahobilam Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy Temple (Nava Narasimha)
summary: Group of nine Narasimha shrines in the Nallamala forest at Ahobilam, held to be where Vishnu as Narasimha appeared to save Prahlada. It is one of the 108 Divya Desams.
history: Ahobilam is praised in the hymns of the 9th-century Alvar Thirumangai. The site gained prominence between the 12th and 16th centuries, with inscriptions recording patronage from the Kakatiya and Reddi rulers and, later, the Saluva and Tuluva kings of Vijayanagara, who built the large Prahladavarada temple complex in Lower Ahobilam. The shrines are traditionally administered by the Ahobila Mutt, founded here in the 14th century.
significance: Pilgrims visit the nine Narasimha shrines (Jwala, Ahobila, Malola, Kroda, Karanja, Bhargava, Yogananda, Chatravata and Pavana), several reached by forest treks in Upper Ahobilam, about 8 km from Lower Ahobilam. The Ugra Stambham is pointed out as the pillar from which Narasimha emerged. The annual Brahmotsavam is held around February-March, and Narasimha Jayanti is also celebrated.

summary: Shiva temple set against the Erramala hills near Banaganapalle, where Shiva and Parvati are worshipped as Uma Maheswara in a single stone. It is known for its 'growing' Nandi and nearby caves.
history: Legend says the sage Agastya intended to build a Venkateswara temple here, but the idol was found damaged, so on Shiva's advice the site became a Shiva shrine. The present temple is attributed to the Sangama kings of the Vijayanagara empire in the 15th century. Another legend tells of the devotee Chitteppa, who saw Shiva in the form of a tiger.
significance: Devotees believe the large Nandi in front of the temple has grown over the years, to the point that a pillar was removed. Nearby caves include the Agastya cave, reached by about 120 steps, and the Venkateswara cave with the damaged idol. Bathing in the Pushkarini fed by a perennial spring precedes worship. Maha Shivaratri (February-March) is the main festival.

The mutt that grew around the Brindavana is run by the Sri Raghavendra Swamy Matha. Tradition also holds that the site is where Prahlada performed a yagna in an earlier age.

The three-day Aradhana marking the saint's entry into the Brindavana (Shravana month, usually August) is the biggest event. The village goddess Manchalamma is worshipped before visiting the Brindavana.

name: Veerabhadra Temple, Lepakshi
summary: 16th-century Vijayanagara temple of Veerabhadra on the Kurma Saila rock at Lepakshi, known for its hanging pillar, ceiling murals and the huge monolithic Nandi nearby.
history: The temple was built around 1530-1540, during the reign of Achyuta Deva Raya, by the brothers Virupanna and Veeranna, officials of the Vijayanagara empire at Penukonda. A popular legend says Virupanna was punished for spending treasury funds on it. Tradition links the name Lepakshi to the Ramayana, where Rama told the wounded bird Jatayu to rise ('le pakshi'). It is a centrally protected monument under the Archaeological Survey of India.
significance: The temple is visited both for worship of Veerabhadra and for its art: fresco paintings on the ceilings, the unfinished Kalyana Mandapa, a large naga-linga carved from rock, and a pillar that does not fully touch the ground. The monolithic Nandi about 200 m away is among the largest in India. Maha Shivaratri (February-March) is celebrated.

name: Kadiri Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy Temple
summary: Temple of Lord Narasimha in Kadiri town, where tradition says the deity emerged from the roots of a khadri (khadira) tree. It is known for its large annual chariot festival.
history: Legend holds that Narasimha appeared here as a self-manifested form from the roots of a khadri tree to slay Hiranyakashipu, and the town takes its name from the tree. The sage Bhrigu is said to have been entrusted with the deity's worship, and the processional images are known as Vasantha Vallabha because they were installed in spring. The present temple has Vijayanagara-period structures and is administered by the AP Endowments Department.
significance: Devotees believe the main idol perspires after the daily abhishekam. The annual Brahmotsavam in March-April (Phalguna-Chaitra) culminates in the Brahma Rathotsavam, in which a very large wooden chariot is pulled through town while devotees throw pepper, fruit and davanam onto it; lakhs of people attend. Narasimha Jayanti is also celebrated.

name: Vontimitta Sri Kodandarama Swamy Temple
summary: 16th-century Vijayanagara temple of Rama near Kadapa, where Rama, Sita and Lakshmana are carved from a single stone. It is run by TTD and hosts the state's official Sri Rama Navami celebrations.
history: The temple dates to the 16th century and shows Vijayanagara architecture, including a large Ranga Mandapa with 32 carved pillars. Local legend credits two reformed robbers, Vontudu and Mittudu, with building it in a single day, giving the village its name. The poet Bammera Potana, author of the Telugu Bhagavatam, and Vavilakolanu Subba Rao (known as Andhra Valmiki) are associated with the temple. It is a centrally protected monument and has been administered by TTD since 2015.
significance: Because Sita, Rama and Lakshmana share one stone, the place is also called Ekasila Nagaram, and the temple is noted for having no separate Hanuman idol in the sanctum. The annual Brahmotsavam in Chaitra (March-April) includes Sri Sita Rama Kalyanam, which is performed at night under the full moon. Since 2015 the Andhra Pradesh government has held its official Sri Rama Navami celebrations here.

name: Penchalakona Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy Temple
summary: Forest temple of a self-manifested Narasimha in the Velikonda hills near Rapur, where the deity is worshipped with Chenchu Lakshmi.
history: Legend says that after slaying Hiranyakashipu, the still-fierce Narasimha was calmed here by Lakshmi, born as Chenchu Lakshmi, the daughter of a Chenchu tribal chief, whom he married. The deity is regarded as self-manifested in rock, and the temple is said to have been renovated in the 10th century. The nearby stream, Kanvaleru, is today known as the Kandaleru.
significance: Devotees regard it as one of the Narasimha kshetras of Andhra Pradesh and visit the hill shrine amid forest streams. The annual Brahmotsavam in Vaisakha (April-May), coinciding with Narasimha Jayanti, includes Dhwajarohanam, vahana sevas and Chakra Snanam; many people in the region abstain from non-vegetarian food during the festival.

rules.dress_code: Traditional or modest Indian attire is expected; shorts and sleeveless clothing are discouraged.

name: Sri Kalyana Venkateswara Swamy Temple, Narayanavanam
summary: TTD-run temple at Narayanavanam, held to be the place where Lord Venkateswara married Padmavathi, daughter of King Akasa Raju.
history: Narayanavanam is traditionally identified as the capital of King Akasa Raju, and the temple is said to mark the spot where his daughter Padmavathi married Lord Venkateswara before the couple went to Tirumala. The temple is recorded as established in 1541 CE. It is administered by Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams. The complex includes a shrine of Agastheeswara Swamy and the grinding stone said to have been used for the wedding preparations.
significance: Couples visit to seek blessings for marriage, as the temple commemorates the divine wedding. The annual Brahmotsavam and the Kalyanotsavam are the main celebrations, and the Agastheeswara shrine in the complex holds its own Brahmotsavam in April.

rules.dress_code: Traditional Indian attire is expected: dhoti or kurta-pyjama / trousers with shirt for men, saree or salwar kameez with dupatta for women.

name: Sri Vedanarayana Swamy Temple, Nagalapuram
summary: Vijayanagara-era temple of Vishnu in his Matsya (fish) incarnation at Nagalapuram, known for the annual Surya Puja when the setting sun's rays reach the deity.
history: The temple honours Matsya, who according to legend recovered the Vedas stolen by the demon Somakasura and hidden in the ocean. Krishnadevaraya of Vijayanagara is credited with building much of the present complex, including its seven gateways and five enclosures, and with renaming the town Nagalapuram after his mother Nagamamba. The temple is administered by Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams.
significance: The image of Matsya faces west, and during the Surya Puja festival in Phalguna (around March) the rays of the setting sun fall on the deity's feet, navel and forehead on three successive days. The annual Brahmotsavam is held around the same time. Devotees visit as one of the few temples dedicated to the Matsya avatar.

rules.dress_code: Traditional Indian attire is expected: dhoti or kurta-pyjama / trousers with shirt for men, saree or salwar kameez with dupatta for women.

pujas.name: Surya Pujotsavam
pujas.description: Festival during which the setting sun's rays fall on the deity.

pujas.name: Kalyanotsavam
pujas.description: Ritual wedding of the processional deities.

name: Sri Kanaka Durga Temple, Vijayawada
summary: Hilltop shrine of Goddess Kanaka Durga on Indrakeeladri above the Krishna river in Vijayawada, worshipped together with Shiva as Malleswara Swamy; one of the most visited temples in Andhra Pradesh.
history: Tradition links the hill to the sage Indrakila, who asked the goddess to reside on him, and to Durga's victory over Mahishasura. The Mahabharata episode in which Arjuna performed penance for the Pasupatastra is also located on Indrakeeladri. A Telugu inscription of 1229 CE refers to the shrine of Bejawada Malleswaradeva at Indrakiladri, the earliest dated reference. Temple tradition holds that Adi Shankaracharya installed a Sri Chakra here. The temple is administered by the Sri Durga Malleswara Swamyvarla Devasthanam.
significance: Devotees come for darshan of the goddess, believed to be swayambhu, and to fulfil vows. The biggest festival is Dasara (Sharan Navaratri) in Ashvayuja (September-October), when the goddess is adorned in a different alankaram each day; Moola Nakshatram during Navaratri is treated as her birth-star day and draws the largest crowds, and the festival closes with a float festival (Teppotsavam) on the Krishna. The Bhavani Deeksha season and the Ashada month offering of saris (Ashada Sare) are other major observances.

rules.dress_code: Traditional attire expected: saree or churidar for women; dhoti, kurta-pyjama or shirt and trousers for men. Shorts, mini-skirts and sleeveless tops are not allowed (temple rule reported 2018).
rules.mobile: Mobile phones and cameras are not allowed inside; counters/lockers are available near the foot of the hill.
rules.queue: Free Dharma darshan plus paid Mukha Mandapam and Antaralayam darshan queues; very long waits during Dasara.

pujas.description: Worship of the Sri Chakra through its nine enclosures.

pujas.description: Free meals for devotees.

name: Sri Panakala Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy Temple, Mangalagiri
summary: Narasimha shrine on Mangalagiri hill where the deity is offered panakam (jaggery water) and is believed to accept only half of each offering; a second Lakshmi Narasimha temple with a tall gopuram stands at the foot of the hill.
history: Local legend says Narasimha manifested here to destroy the demon Namuchi, and that the hill shrine has a mouth-shaped opening into which devotees pour panakam. The temple at the foot of the hill dedicated to Lakshmi Narasimha has an 11-storey gopuram about 47 m (153 ft) high, raised by Raja Vasireddy Venkatadri Nayudu in 1807-1809. It is regarded as one of the tallest gopurams in South India.
significance: Pilgrims climb the hill to offer panakam to Panakala Narasimha; whatever the quantity offered, about half is believed to be accepted and the rest returned as prasadam. The hill shrine is open only until early afternoon, as it is believed the devas worship the Lord later in the day. The annual Brahmotsavam runs for 11 days in Phalguna (February-March), from Phalguna Shuddha Shashti to Purnima, with the Kalyanotsavam on Phalguna Shuddha Chaturdashi.

pujas.name: Panakam offering
pujas.description: Jaggery water poured into the mouth of the deity by priests on behalf of devotees.

pujas.name: Kalyanotsavam
pujas.description: Celestial wedding of Lakshmi and Narasimha.
pujas.schedule_note: Annually on Phalguna Shuddha Chaturdashi during Brahmotsavam

name: Sri Amareswara Swamy Temple, Amaravati
address: Amaravathi, on the south bank of the Krishna river
summary: One of the five Pancharama Shiva temples, on the south bank of the Krishna at Amaravathi, known for a very tall white linga whose abhishekam is performed from an upper floor.
history: Temple legend holds that the Shiva linga of Tarakasura was shattered by Kumaraswamy (Subrahmanya) and its five pieces fell at five places in Andhra, which became the Pancharama Kshetras. Here the linga is said to have been installed by Indra, giving the name Amareswara. The present temple is dated to around the 11th century. Krishnadevaraya is recorded as having presented gifts to the deity after taking Kondavidu in 1515, and Raja Vasireddy Venkatadri Nayudu, who moved to Amaravathi in 1796, carried out major restoration of the temple.
significance: As one of the Pancharamas it is part of the five-temple circuit undertaken especially in the Karthika month (October-November). The linga is about 15 feet tall, so priests perform abhishekam from the upper storey. Main festivals are Maha Shivaratri (February-March), Karthika Purnima and Navaratri, along with kalyanotsavams.

pujas.name: Abhishekam
pujas.description: Ritual bathing of the linga, performed from the upper floor because of its height.
pujas.schedule_note: Daily; extended hours in Karthika masam

name: Sri Bhimeswara Swamy Temple, Draksharamam
summary: Pancharama Shiva temple of Bhimeswara Swamy at Draksharamam, which also houses Goddess Manikyamba, counted among the Ashtadasa (18) Shakti Peethas.
history: Temple legend holds that the Shiva linga of Tarakasura was shattered by Kumaraswamy (Subrahmanya) and its five pieces fell at five places in Andhra, which became the Pancharama Kshetras. The town's name is linked to Daksha Prajapati, whose sacrifice is placed here in the Skanda Purana; the left cheek of Sati is believed to have fallen here, worshipped as Manikyamba. Temple inscriptions attribute construction to the Eastern Chalukya king Bhima in the 9th-10th centuries CE, and the temple has many later inscriptions from the 11th century onwards.
significance: The temple is visited both as a Pancharama and as a Shakti Peetha, and is sometimes called Dakshina Kashi. The tall linga rises through a two-level sanctum, and devotees climb to the upper level to view its top. Maha Shivaratri (February-March), when hours are extended, and Karthika masam (October-November) including Karthika Purnima are the main festivals; Navaratri is observed at the Manikyamba shrine.

pujas.name: Abhishekam
pujas.description: Ritual bathing of the Bhimeswara linga.

nearest.railway: Kakinada, about 28 km; Rajahmundry, about 50 km

name: Sri Ksheera Ramalingeswara Swamy Temple, Palakollu
summary: One of the five Pancharama Shiva temples, at Palakollu, known for its milk-white linga and a nine-storey gopuram about 120 feet tall.
history: Temple legend holds that the Shiva linga of Tarakasura was shattered by Kumaraswamy (Subrahmanya) and its five pieces fell at five places in Andhra, which became the Pancharama Kshetras. The name Ksheerarama ('milk grove') comes from the legend that milk sprang from the ground here when Shiva struck it. The temple dates from the Eastern Chalukya period (about the 9th-10th centuries, with some sources citing 11th-century epigraphy), and the tall gopuram was added in the 14th century by Alladu Reddy.
significance: Devotees visit as part of the Pancharama circuit, especially in Karthika masam (October-November). The nine-storey, roughly 120-foot gopuram is among the tallest in Andhra Pradesh. Maha Shivaratri (February-March) and Karthika festivals are the main celebrations.

pujas.name: Abhishekam
pujas.description: Ritual bathing of the Ksheera Ramalingeswara linga.

name: Sri Someswara Swamy Temple, Bhimavaram
summary: Pancharama Shiva temple at Gunupudi in Bhimavaram whose linga is said to change colour with the lunar cycle, appearing dark on new moon and white on full moon.
history: Temple legend holds that the Shiva linga of Tarakasura was shattered by Kumaraswamy (Subrahmanya) and its five pieces fell at five places in Andhra, which became the Pancharama Kshetras. The local legend says Chandra (Soma), cursed to lose his glow, installed the linga here on Shiva's advice, hence the name Someswara. The present temple with its gopuram and prakara is attributed to the Eastern Chalukya king Chalukya Bhima, generally placed in the 9th century, though sources differ on the date.
significance: Pilgrims come to see the linga, said to turn black-brown around Amavasya and white around Pournami. The shrine of Annapurna is on the upper floor above the sanctum. Maha Shivaratri (February-March) and Sharan Navaratri (September-October) are the main festivals, and Karthika masam brings Pancharama pilgrims. The temple is closed during solar and lunar eclipses.

pujas.name: Abhishekam
pujas.description: Ritual bathing of the Someswara linga.

name: Sri Kumara Bhimeswara Swamy Temple, Samalkot
summary: Pancharama Shiva temple at Samalkot built by the Eastern Chalukyas in the 9th century, with a monolithic linga that rises through two storeys and a monolithic Nandi.
history: Temple legend holds that the Shiva linga of Tarakasura was shattered by Kumaraswamy (Subrahmanya) and its five pieces fell at five places in Andhra, which became the Pancharama Kshetras. The linga here is believed to have been installed by Kumaraswamy himself, hence Kumararama. The temple was built by the Eastern Chalukya king Chalukya Bhima I towards the end of the 9th century; inscriptions call the village Chalukya Bhimavaram. It closely resembles the Draksharamam temple built by the same dynasty.
significance: The tall monolithic linga rises from the ground floor and passes through the roof into the upper storey, where devotees view its top. Goddess Bala Tripura Sundari is the consort. Maha Shivaratri (February-March) is the most important festival, and Karthika masam brings Pancharama pilgrims.

pujas.name: Abhishekam
pujas.description: Ritual bathing of the Kumara Bhimeswara linga.

name: Sri Veera Venkata Satyanarayana Swamy Temple, Annavaram
summary: Hilltop temple of Lord Satyanarayana on Ratnagiri above the Pampa river at Annavaram, best known as the centre for performing the Satyanarayana Vratam.
history: According to temple tradition, the idol was found on Ratnagiri hill in 1891 after a local zamindar, Raja Ramanarayanam, had a dream, and a small shrine was set up that year. The main temple was rebuilt in 1933-34 in the form of a chariot with four wheels, and was renovated again in 2011-12. The deity is worshipped in a combined form with Lakshmi and Shiva alongside Satyanarayana.
significance: Thousands of devotees come daily, many to perform the Satyanarayana Vratam in the temple's vratam halls, especially newly married couples and during Karthika masam (October-November), when crowds peak. Major festivals include the Kalyanotsavam and Vaisakha Ekadasi (April-May) and Bhishma Ekadasi (January-February). The hill can be reached by road or by a stepped path from the base.

rules.dress_code: A traditional dress code was announced in 2019: dhoti for men and saree, half-saree or churidar with dupatta for women, applied first to devotees performing vratams and rituals.
rules.queue: Free Sarva darshan plus special entry darshan; vratams are performed in batches through the day.

pujas.description: The Satyanarayana Swamy vratam performed by devotees with priests in the temple's vratam halls.

pujas.description: Morning awakening ritual of the deity.

pujas.description: Daily celestial wedding of the Lord and Ammavaru.

name: Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy Temple, Antarvedi
summary: Lakshmi Narasimha temple at Antarvedi, near the point where the Vasishta Godavari meets the Bay of Bengal, famous for its annual Kalyanam festival and chariot procession in Magha.
history: Legend says Sage Vasishta had his ashram here and that Narasimha appeared to slay a demon at his request, after which the deity was installed. The earlier temple was threatened and eventually lost to coastal erosion, while the idol survived; the present temple is credited to Koppanathi Krishnamma, who built it in 1823 (Saka 1745). Some sources place an older structure in the 15th-16th centuries.
significance: Pilgrims bathe at the Sagara Sangamam, the confluence of the Vasishta Godavari with the sea, before darshan. The main event is the 10-day Kalyana Mahotsavam of Lakshmi and Narasimha in Magha (usually late January-February), from Magha Shuddha Saptami, with the Kalyanam on the eve of Bhishma Ekadashi and a large chariot festival. The temple area also has a lighthouse and beach that draw visitors.

pujas.name: Kalyanotsavam
pujas.description: Celestial wedding of Lakshmi and Narasimha.
pujas.schedule_note: Annual main festival in Magha; also performed as a seva

name: Sri Venkateswara Swamy Temple, Dwaraka Tirumala
summary: Hillock temple of Lord Venkateswara at Dwaraka Tirumala, popularly called Chinna Tirupati, a major pilgrimage centre for the Godavari districts.
history: The place is named after Sage Dwaraka, who is said to have found the self-manifested idol of Venkateswara in an anthill after long penance. Because only the upper half of that idol is visible, a second, full idol was installed later, so the sanctum has two images of the Lord. The vimana, mantapa, gopuram and prakara are credited to the local ruler Dharma Appa Rao (1762-c.1827), and a queen of Mylavaram donated gold ornaments and silver vahanas.
significance: Devotees who cannot travel to Tirumala often fulfil their vows here, including tonsuring. The temple draws about 50 lakh visitors a year. Two Brahmotsavams are held each year, in Vaisakha (April-May) and Ashvayuja (September-October), for the swayambhu and installed idols respectively; Vaikunta Ekadasi and Ratha Saptami are other major days.

pujas.name: Suprabhatam
pujas.description: Morning awakening ritual of the Lord.

pujas.name: Ekantha Seva
pujas.description: Night ritual that closes the day.

name: Sri Siddhi Vinayaka Swamy Temple, Ainavilli
summary: Ancient Ganesha temple at Ainavilli in Konaseema, where the deity, also called Vigneswara Swamy, faces south; a popular place to begin new ventures.
history: The kshetra purana says Daksha Prajapati worshipped Vinayaka here for the success of his yagna before performing it at nearby Draksharamam. Another tradition holds that Sage Vyasa installed the Ganapati here before his journey through South India. The date of the present structure is not recorded in available sources.
significance: Devotees pray here before starting new work, education or business, and the south-facing deity is believed to grant prosperity. The biggest festival is the Vinayaka Chavithi Navaratri in Bhadrapada (August-September), which draws tens of thousands of devotees over nine days.

name: Sri Venkateswara Swamy Temple, Vadapalli
address: Vadapalle, Atreyapuram mandal, on the Gautami Godavari
summary: Venkateswara temple at Vadapalle on the Godavari in Konaseema, notable for its main deity carved from red sandalwood and for the vow of visiting on seven Saturdays.
history: The temple was built in 1759 by Pinapotu Gajendrudu, according to Wikipedia. Unlike most Venkateswara temples, the presiding deity is carved from red sandalwood rather than stone. The village, once a river port, was earlier known as Odapalli or Naukapuri ('town of boats').
significance: The deity is worshipped as Kalyana Venkateswara, and devotees seeking marriage and other wishes visit on seven consecutive Saturdays and walk eleven pradakshinas around the shrine. Saturdays draw very large crowds, and the temple has become one of the busiest in the Godavari delta. APTDC runs pilgrimage tours to the temple from Vijayawada.

rules.queue: Saturdays are by far the busiest day; many devotees arrive before sunrise.

pujas.name: Kalyanam
pujas.description: Celestial wedding of the Lord, offered by devotees praying for marriage.

name: Sri Jagan Mohini Kesava Swamy Temple, Ryali
summary: Vishnu temple at Ryali in Konaseema whose single black-stone idol shows Kesava on the front and Mohini on the back, with a small spring of water at the deity's feet.
history: The sthala purana links Ryali to Vishnu's Mohini avatar during the churning of the ocean: a flower from Mohini's hair is said to have fallen here, and 'ryali' is taken to mean 'fall' in Telugu. Local tradition says a king rediscovered the buried idol after a dream and built the shrine in the 11th century, though this is not documented. Facing it is the Uma Kamandaleswara Swamy temple, where Brahma is believed to have worshipped the linga with water from his kamandalam.
significance: Devotees come to see the unusual two-sided idol, about 5 by 3 feet, carved from one stone, and the water that seeps from beneath the deity's feet and is sprinkled on pilgrims as Ganga. The annual Kalyanotsavam is celebrated for five days in March-April. The village lies between the Vasishta and Gautami branches of the Godavari.

pujas.name: Kalyanotsavam
pujas.description: Celestial wedding festival of the Lord.

name: Sri Subrahmanya Swamy Temple, Mopidevi
summary: Temple of Subrahmanyeswara Swamy at Mopidevi in Krishna district, worshipped in serpent form and widely visited for Sarpa (Naga) dosha nivarana rituals.
history: One legend says Sage Agastya found Subrahmanya doing penance here in the form of a serpent and installed a linga. Another local account says a devotee from the potter community, Veeravarapu Parvathalu, saw the deity in a vision emerging from an anthill, leading to the shrine. The main deity is a self-manifested form, and the temple was long associated with the zamindars of Challapalli.
significance: Couples facing delays in marriage or childlessness and people seeking relief from Sarpa, Rahu-Ketu and related doshas perform rituals here. Major festivals are Subrahmanya Shashti (Margashira, November-December), Skanda Shashti and Nagula Chavithi (Karthika, October-November). Sundays and Tuesdays are the busiest days.

rules.queue: Sundays and Tuesdays are the busiest days.

pujas.name: Sarpa Dosha Nivarana Puja
pujas.description: Ritual for relief from serpent-related doshas.

pujas.name: Rahu-Ketu Dosha Puja
pujas.description: Ritual to propitiate Rahu and Ketu.

pujas.name: Abhishekam
pujas.description: Ritual bathing of the deity.

name: Sri Trikoteswara Swamy Temple, Kotappakonda
summary: Hilltop Shiva temple on the Brahma peak of Kotappakonda (Trikutadri) near Narasaraopet, home to one of the largest Maha Shivaratri jataras in Andhra Pradesh.
history: The hill has three peaks associated with Brahma, Vishnu and Rudra, hence the names Trikutadri and Trikoteswara. Tradition says Shiva first resided on Rudra Shikharam, where the old Kotayya temple stands, and moved to the present site in response to the devotion of Anandavalli (Gollabhama). Shiva is worshipped here in the Dakshinamurthy form. The date of the present structure is not established in available sources.
significance: The Maha Shivaratri jatara (February-March) draws huge crowds, with villages bringing tall decorated structures called prabhalu to the hill. Devotees also visit the Paapanaseswara shrine on Vishnu Shikharam and the old Kotayya temple on Rudra Shikharam. The hill is reachable by ghat road and by steps.

pujas.name: Abhishekam
pujas.description: Ritual bathing of the linga.

name: Sri Kukkuteswara Swamy Temple & Puruhutika Devi, Pithapuram
summary: Temple complex at Pithapuram combining the Kukkuteswara (Shiva) shrine, the Puruhutika Devi shrine counted among the 18 Maha Shakti Peethas, and the sacred Pada Gaya tank.
history: Shiva is worshipped here as Kukkuteswara, a linga in the form of a rooster. Local lore ties the Pada Gaya tank to the demon Gayasura, whose feet are said to rest here, making Pithapuram one of the three Gaya kshetras with Gaya and Siro Gaya. The Puruhutika shrine in the north-east of the complex marks the spot where, in Shakta tradition, a part of Sati's body fell (sources differ on which); the town's old names Puruhutikapuram and Pithikapuri derive from it.
significance: The complex is important to both Shaiva and Shakta devotees, and pilgrims bathe in the Pada Gaya tank, where ancestral rites are believed to be as meritorious as at Kashi. Navaratri (September-October) is the main festival at the Puruhutika shrine and Maha Shivaratri (February-March) at Kukkuteswara. Pithapuram is also revered as the birthplace of Sripada Srivallabha, regarded as an incarnation of Dattatreya, and the complex has a Dattatreya shrine.

name: Sri Andhra Maha Vishnu Temple, Srikakulam
address: Srikakulam village, Ghantasala mandal, near the Krishna river
summary: Ancient Vishnu temple at Srikakulam village in Krishna district, dedicated to Andhra Maha Vishnu (Telugu Vallabha), closely associated with Krishnadevaraya's Telugu poem Amuktamalyada.
history: Tradition holds that the shrine dates back to the Satavahana period and that Srikakulam was an early seat of Andhra rulers. Krishnadevaraya stayed here during his Kalinga campaign, and in the Amuktamalyada he describes the deity appearing to him in a dream and asking him to compose a work in Telugu. After a period of decline, the Zamindars of Challapalli repaired the temple and restored worship, moved by a satakam on the deity by the poet Kasula Purushottama Kavi.
significance: The temple is valued as a symbol of Telugu identity, since the deity is regarded as the patron of the Andhra people and the inspiration for Amuktamalyada. It is a quiet village temple rather than a major crowd-drawing shrine. Note this is Srikakulam in Krishna district, about 44 km from Vijayawada, not the northern district headquarters of the same name.

name: Sri Mavullamma Ammavari Temple, Bhimavaram
address: Sunday Market area, Kuriseti Vari Street, Gandhinagar, Bhimavaram
summary: Temple of Goddess Mavullamma, the village goddess (grama devata) of Bhimavaram, in the busy market area at the heart of the town.
history: Local tradition says the goddess manifested around 1200 CE in a mango grove, giving the name Mamillamma, later Mavullamma. Her original spot is said to have been under a pipal and neem tree in Motupallivari Street. Around 1880, according to tradition, the goddess asked Grandhi Appanna in a dream to build a temple for her, and the present shrine dates from that period.
significance: Mavullamma is the guardian deity of Bhimavaram and is worshipped by the whole town, with an annual jatara and utsavams that draw thousands of devotees. Devotees offer saris and other vows, and the temple is usually visited together with the Somarama temple about 2 km away.

name: Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy Temple, Vedadri
address: Vedadri, Jaggayyapeta mandal, on the Krishna river
summary: Narasimha temple on a hillock by the Krishna river at Vedadri, known as a Pancha Narasimha Kshetram where five forms of Narasimha are worshipped.
history: The sthala purana says the demon Somakasura stole the Vedas, and Vishnu recovered them; the Vedas took the form of this hill (Veda-adri) and asked the Lord to stay, and he remained as Narasimha. The temple gained importance under the Kakatiyas, and the saint-composer Narayana Tirtha is said to have visited regularly. In the 1800s Raja Vasireddy Muktiswara Prasad Nayudu renovated the temple, renewed the dhwajasthambham and built 108 steps from the hillock down to the river.
significance: Devotees worship five forms: Yogananda Lakshmi Narasimha (main deity), Jwala Narasimha on the hilltop, Salagrama Narasimha in the river, Veera Narasimha and Lakshmi Narasimha. Pilgrims bathe in the Krishna before darshan. Narasimha Jayanti on Vaisakha Shuddha Purnima (April-May) is the main annual festival.

name: Sri Bhavannarayana Swamy Temple, Bapatla
summary: Ancient Vishnu temple of Ksheera Bhavanarayana Swamy and his consort Sundaravalli at Bapatla, after which the town is named; it is a protected monument.
history: The town's name is derived from the temple: Bhavapuri became Bhavapatla and then Bapatla. Local sthala purana credits a Chola ruler with building the temple and its large gopuram, and Wikipedia records construction in 1465 by a Chola king named Krimikantha Chola, with later restoration; other sources claim much greater antiquity. Accounts of the date therefore differ. The temple is under the protection of the Archaeological Survey of India.
significance: The temple is the main religious landmark of Bapatla and is visited by devotees of Vishnu as Bhavanarayana with Goddess Sundaravalli; it also has a shrine of Venugopala Swamy. It is regarded as one of the Pancha Bhavanarayana kshetras of coastal Andhra.

name: Sri Varaha Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy Temple, Simhachalam
summary: Hilltop temple near Visakhapatnam where Vishnu is worshipped in a combined Varaha-Narasimha form, the idol kept covered in sandalwood paste for all but one day a year.
history: Local legend links the shrine to Prahlada, who is said to have built the first temple after Narasimha saved him. Inscriptions show that Kulottunga Chola I made endowments here in the late 11th century. The present stone temple is attributed to the Eastern Ganga king Narasimha Deva I, with consecration under his son Bhanudeva I around 1268 CE. Krishnadevaraya of Vijayanagara visited in 1516. Since 1949 the temple has been administered by the state, with the Pusapati Gajapati family of Vizianagaram as hereditary trustees.
significance: Simhachalam is one of the most visited Vaishnava shrines in Andhra Pradesh, and the deity is popularly called Simhadri Appanna. The idol stays coated in sandalwood paste through the year and its original form (nijaroopa darshan) is shown only on Akshaya Tritiya, during the Chandanotsavam festival in April-May. Other major events are the annual Kalyanotsavam in spring and the Giri Pradakshina, a circumambulation of the hill on foot before Ashadha Purnima. Devotees also embrace the Kappa Stambham pillar in the temple, believed to grant children and cure illnesses.

pujas.name: Suprabhata Seva
pujas.description: Early-morning awakening service for the deity.

pujas.name: Nitya Kalyanam
pujas.description: Daily celestial wedding ceremony of the deity with Lakshmi.

pujas.name: Chandanotsavam (Nijaroopa Darshan)
pujas.description: Annual removal of the sandalwood coating to reveal the original form of the deity.

name: Sri Suryanarayana Swamy Temple, Arasavalli
summary: Ancient temple to the Sun god on the outskirts of Srikakulam, aligned so that the early-morning sun falls on the idol on a few days each year.
history: Tradition, citing the Padma Purana, credits the sage Kashyapa with installing the deity. Inscriptions are generally read as showing the temple was established by the Eastern Ganga (Kalinga) king Devendra Varma around the 7th century. The shrine suffered damage in later centuries and was rebuilt in the late 18th century, an account naming Yelamanchili Pullaji Panthulu as the restorer around 1778. It is one of the few actively worshipped Surya temples in India.
significance: Devotees come to pray for health, especially relief from eye and skin ailments, and many offer Surya Namaskarams. Ratha Saptami in January-February is the main festival, drawing very large crowds; the state declared it a state festival in 2024. The temple is oriented so that sunlight touches the feet of the idol for a few minutes in the early morning twice a year, around March and October. Sundays are considered especially auspicious for worship here.

pujas.name: Ksheerabhishekam
pujas.description: Milk ablution of the deity, especially performed on Ratha Saptami.

pujas.name: Surya Namaskaram
pujas.description: Prostrations and prayers offered to the Sun god by devotees.

name: Sri Kurmanatha Swamy Temple, Srikurmam
summary: Rare temple to Vishnu in his Kurma (tortoise) avatar near Srikakulam, known for its rows of carved single-stone pillars and old murals.
history: Legend says the tortoise form of Vishnu manifested here for a king named Sweta Chakravarthi. Inscriptions record that the Eastern Ganga king Anantavarman Chodaganga Deva turned an earlier Shiva shrine into a Vaishnava one, a change linked to the visit of Ramanuja. The Eastern Ganga king Anangabhima Deva III built the circumambulatory mandapa. In the 13th century Naraharitirtha, a disciple of Madhvacharya, made Srikurmam a centre of Vaishnava activity, and the temple later passed under the Gajapatis of Odisha.
significance: It is regarded as one of the very few temples in the world where Vishnu is worshipped as Kurma. The walkway is lined with 108 monolithic pillars, none identical, and the walls carry old paintings. The three-day Dolotsavam in Phalguna (February-March) is the main festival, and Kurma Jayanti is also observed. Pilgrims also perform rites for ancestors at the Sweta Pushkarini tank, and the temple keeps a sanctuary for star tortoises.

pujas.name: Rajabhogam
pujas.description: Midday food offering to the deity.

pujas.name: Pavalimpu Seva

name: Sri Mukhalingeswara Temple, Srimukhalingam
summary: Group of early Kalinga-style Shiva temples on the Vamsadhara river at the former Eastern Ganga capital of Kalinganagari, noted for fine stone carving.
history: Srimukhalingam, then known as Kalinganagari, was a capital of the Eastern Ganga dynasty for several centuries before Anantavarman Chodaganga moved the capital to Odisha in the 12th century. The main Madhukeswara (Mukhalingeswara) temple is attributed to the Eastern Ganga king Kamarnava Deva, and the nearby Someswara and Bhimeswara temples belong to the same period. Historians date the three temples between the late 8th and early 11th century CE.
significance: The main linga is said to bear a face of Shiva, which gives the place its name. The temples are valued for their early Kalinga architecture, perforated stone windows and sculptures, including images linked to the Pashupata sect. Maha Shivaratri in February-March is the main festival, celebrated as a Brahmotsavam that ends with the Chakratheertha Snanam, a ritual dip in the Vamsadhara.

pujas.name: Maha Shivaratri Brahmotsavam
pujas.description: Annual festival around Maha Shivaratri with processions and special worship.

pujas.name: Chakratheertha Snanam
pujas.description: Ritual bath of the deity in the Vamsadhara river that concludes the Shivaratri festival.

name: Sri Kanaka Mahalakshmi Temple, Visakhapatnam
summary: Roofless temple of Kanaka Mahalakshmi, the guardian goddess of Visakhapatnam, in the old town at Burujupeta, where devotees may worship the idol themselves.
history: The goddess is believed to be self-manifested and was once the family deity of the local rulers, standing within the old Burujupeta fort. Tradition says the idol was thrown into a well during an attack and later recovered; accounts date the recovery and the present shrine to the early 20th century. Locals say a plague followed when the idol was moved and eased once it was returned, and the goddess is said to have asked in a dream to remain without a roof.
significance: The temple has no roof over the deity and devotees are allowed to perform puja to the idol with their own hands. The month-long Margasira Masotsavam (roughly December) is the main festival, with Thursdays drawing huge crowds. Varalakshmi Vratham in Shravana and Friday Lakshmi pujas are also popular.

rules.entry: Open to all devotees, who may personally offer worship to the idol.

pujas.name: Panchamruta Abhishekam
pujas.description: Ablution of the goddess with five sacred substances, followed by Sahasranamarchana.

pujas.description: Thursday worship of the goddess during the Margasira festival month.

pujas.description: Special Lakshmi worship by women in Shravana month.

name: Sri Sampath Vinayagar Temple, Visakhapatnam
summary: Popular Ganesha temple at Asilmetta in central Visakhapatnam, built in 1962 and now run by the Endowments Department.
history: The temple was built in 1962 by the brothers T.S. Rajeshwaran and T.S. Selvaganesan, originally as a small shrine within their business premises, and later came under the Andhra Pradesh Endowments Department. In 1967 the Kanchi Shankaracharya Chandrasekharendra Saraswati is said to have installed a Ganapati yantra here. Local belief links the temple to the 1971 war, when naval officers prayed here before the Pakistani submarine Ghazi sank off Visakhapatnam.
significance: It is one of the most visited temples in the city, and many people come to have new vehicles blessed or to start ventures with Ganesha's blessings. Ganesh Chaturthi in August-September is the main festival, drawing large crowds. Tuesdays and Chaturthi days are also busy.

pujas.description: Blessing ritual for newly bought vehicles.

pujas.name: Ganesh Chaturthi celebrations
pujas.description: Annual festival with special abhishekam and decorations for Ganesha.

name: Sri Pydithalli Ammavari Temple, Vizianagaram
summary: Temple of Pydithalli Ammavaru, the guardian village goddess of Vizianagaram, famous for the Sirimanu festival held each October.
history: The goddess is identified with Pydimamba, a sister of the Vizianagaram ruler Pusapati Vijaya Rama Raju. Tradition says she tried to dissuade her brother from the war with Bobbili in 1757 and gave up her life on hearing of his death; her idol was later recovered from a tank after a divine instruction. The shrine dates from the 18th century, though the estate records give no detailed history of its construction.
significance: Pydithalli is worshipped as the grama devata (guardian deity) of Vizianagaram town. The Sirimanu Utsavam, on the first Tuesday after Vijayadasami (October), is the main event: the priest, seated on top of a very tall wooden pole mounted on a cart, is taken three times between the temple and the fort while lakhs of devotees watch. The festival also features the Tolellu ritual the day before and a white elephant chariot recalling the royal family.

pujas.name: Sirimanu Utsavam
pujas.description: Annual procession in which the priest rides atop the tall Sirimanu pole between the temple and the fort.

pujas.name: Tolellu
pujas.description: Ritual on the eve of Sirimanu in which paddy seeds are blessed and distributed to farmers.

name: Ramatheertham Sri Kodanda Rama Swamy Temple, Vizianagaram
summary: Old Rama temple at Ramatheertham, about 12 km from Vizianagaram, set below the Bodikonda hill that also holds Jain and Buddhist remains.
history: Local lore says the idols of Rama, Sita and Lakshmana were found in a sacred pond, which gave the place its name. The site is very old, with Jain caves and a large Buddhist monastery excavated on the surrounding hills, and an inscription of the 5th-century king Indra Bhattaraka Varma has been cited as early evidence of Rama worship here. The present main temple was built by the Pusapati rulers of Vizianagaram after the idols were rediscovered around the 16th century. A small Kodandarama shrine also stands on the Bodikonda hillock; its idol was vandalised in December 2020 and later replaced.
significance: Ramatheertham is the best-known Rama shrine in north Andhra and was even proposed as the venue for the state's official Sri Rama Navami celebration. Sri Rama Navami (March-April), with the Sitarama Kalyanam, is the main festival. Visitors also climb Bodikonda to see the hill shrine, the pond, and the Jain and Buddhist heritage sites.

pujas.name: Sitarama Kalyanam
pujas.description: Celestial wedding of Rama and Sita, celebrated grandly on Sri Rama Navami.

name: Sri Venkateswara Swamy Temple, Upamaka
address: Garudadri hill, Upamaka, Nakkapalli mandal, Anakapalli
summary: Hill temple of Venkateswara on Garudadri near Nakkapalli, where the deity is shown seated on a horse with Lakshmi, facing north.
history: The temple's legend is recorded in the Garudachala Mahatmyam, linked to the Brahma Vaivarta Purana; the hill is said to resemble Garuda, who did penance here. Local accounts credit a king of Kandregula, Sri Krishna Bhupala, with building the temple, though sources give dates ranging from the 6th century to the 11th-12th centuries. The temple is now under the management of TTD.
significance: Upamaka is regarded locally as a northern counterpart of Tirumala, and devotees who cannot travel to Tirupati fulfil vows here. The main festival is the nine-day annual Brahmotsavam in Ashvayuja (around October), with Garuda Vahanam, Rathotsavam and Pallaki Utsavam among the highlights.

pujas.description: Nine-day annual festival with vahana processions, Garuda Seva and the chariot festival.

name: Sri Talupulamma Ammavari Temple, Lova (Tuni)
summary: Forest shrine of the goddess Talupulamma in a valley between two hills at Lova near Tuni, popular with families and with drivers seeking safe journeys.
history: The temple stands in a forested valley between the Darakonda and Teegakonda hillocks. Legend credits the sage Agastya with staying here and naming the hills, and the goddess is believed to roam the hill at night. Reliable records of its construction are not available.
significance: Talupulamma is worshipped as a protective goddess, and many vehicle owners visit to pray for safe travel. An annual 15-day jatara is held in Chaitra (March-April), and the month-long Ashadha festivities (June-July) draw large crowds. The temple closes in the evening because the surrounding hills are forested.

name: Sri Ranganatha Swamy Temple, Nellore (Talpagiri)
address: Ranganayakulapet, on the bank of the Penna river, Nellore
summary: Riverside temple of Ranganatha (reclining Vishnu) on the Penna in Nellore, recognised by its tall entrance gopuram topped with gilded kalasams.
history: Legend tells of a sage who performed a yagna on the bank of the Penna, after which the deity was installed here; one tradition credits a Pallava-era ruler with establishing the shrine around the 7th century. The main shrine and later extensions are attributed to the Chola period around the 12th century. The large entrance tower, known locally as the Gali Gopuram, was built in the 19th century and is credited to Yeragudipati Venkatachalam Panthulu.
significance: It is one of the oldest and most important Vaishnava temples in Nellore city. Vishnu is worshipped here reclining on Adisesha, facing the river. The annual Brahmotsavam in Chaitra (March-April), including the Rathotsavam (chariot festival), is the main celebration, and Vaikuntha Ekadasi also draws large crowds.

pujas.name: Brahmotsavam
pujas.description: Annual festival with daily vahana processions of the deity.

name: Sri Kamakshi Taayi Temple, Jonnawada
summary: Temple of Kamakshi and Mallikarjuna (Shiva) on the north bank of the Penna (Pinakini) about 12 km from Nellore, one of the district's busiest shrines.
history: Tradition holds that the sage Kashyapa performed a great yagna here in the Treta Yuga, which gave the place the name Yagnavatika. A Sri Chakra in the shrine is said to have been installed by Adi Shankaracharya. Accounts of construction differ: the state tourism material cites rock inscriptions crediting a Pallava king Narasimhavarma in the 9th century, while other sources date the temple to around 1150 CE.
significance: Devotees worship Kamakshi as a form of Shakti and Mallikarjuna as Shiva, and bathe in the river at the Kashyapa Theertham before darshan. Many families come to fulfil vows, and Fridays are considered especially auspicious. The Vaisakha Brahmotsavam (April-May) draws lakhs of pilgrims, and Dasara is also celebrated on a large scale.

pujas.name: Vaisakha Brahmotsavam
pujas.description: Annual festival of Mallikarjuna and Kamakshi with processions and a chariot festival.

name: Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy Temple, Narasimha Konda (Vedagiri), Nellore
summary: Hilltop Narasimha temple on Vedagiri, near the Penna river about 15 km from Nellore, associated in legend with sacrifices by the Saptarishis.
history: According to the Puranic legend, the seven sages performed sacrifices on this hill and Narasimha appeared at the end of the yagna; the sage Kashyapa is also linked with the site. Inscriptions are cited as crediting a Pallava king Narasimhavarman with building the temple, though local accounts also describe a foundation about 500 years ago. The goddess here is known as Chenchu Lakshmi, and caves on the hill are associated with Ashwatthama. The state announced development works for the temple in recent years.
significance: Devotees climb the hill for darshan of Narasimha and enjoy views over the Penna valley. The annual Brahmotsavam in May is the main festival. The temple is often visited together with the nearby Jonnawada Kamakshi temple.

pujas.name: Brahmotsavam
pujas.description: Annual festival of the deity with processions.

nearest.bus: Nellore RTC bus station, about 15 km

name: Sri Chennakesava Swamy Temple, Markapur
summary: Vijayanagara-era temple of Chennakesava (Vishnu) in Markapur, known for its very tall gopuram and musical pillars.
history: The sthala purana says that when the demon Kesi troubled sages on the Gundlakamma river, the sage Markandeya appealed to Vishnu, who subdued the demon and settled here as Chennakesava with Lakshmi. The town's name is linked to a milkmaid named Marika, who is said to have built the first small shrine. The temple was greatly expanded in the Vijayanagara period in the 15th-16th centuries, with additions attributed to the reign of Krishnadevaraya, and its walls carry several inscriptions.
significance: The main gopuram, often cited as about 135 feet high, is among the tallest in the Telugu states. The annual Brahmotsavam is held in Phalguna (February-March), with the Ratha Yatra (Tirunalla) as its highlight. The Saptavahana Seva on Ratha Saptami draws very large crowds.

pujas.name: Brahmotsavam
pujas.description: Annual festival of Chennakesava with vahana processions.

name: Sri Tripurantakeswara Swamy Temple, Tripurantakam
address: Tripurantakam, on the Guntur-Srisailam highway, Markapuram
summary: Hill temple of Shiva as Tripurantakeswara, regarded as the eastern gateway to Srisailam, with the Bala Tripura Sundari shrine at its foot.
history: The name comes from the legend of Shiva destroying the demons of Tripura. The site is mentioned in the Skanda Purana and in the hymns of the Tamil Shaiva saint Appar, who lists it as a Vaippu sthalam. Inscriptions indicate development of the temple under Chalukya rulers around the 11th century. A passage on the north side of the temple is traditionally said to lead to Srisailam.
significance: Tripurantakam is counted as the eastern of the four gateways to Srisailam, along with Siddhavatam, Alampur and Umamaheswaram, so pilgrims often visit on the way. The Bala Tripura Sundari temple below the hill has a partly underground sanctum with a Sri Chakra and is revered as a Shakti shrine. Maha Shivaratri (February-March) and Karthika masam are the busiest times.

rules.entry: Public entry into the Bala Tripura Sundari sanctum is restricted.

pujas.name: Maha Shivaratri
pujas.description: Night-long worship and abhishekam of Tripurantakeswara.

nearest.bus: Tripurantakam bus stop on the Guntur-Srisailam highway

name: Bhairavakona Temples (Prakasam)
address: Bhairavakona, near Kothapalli, Chandrasekharapuram mandal, Markapuram
summary: Group of eight rock-cut Shiva cave shrines of the 7th-8th century in the Nallamala hills, beside a waterfall, with a Durga shrine.
history: Eight small cave temples dedicated to different forms of Shiva were cut into a hillside here in the 7th-8th century CE. Their carving closely resembles the rock-cut shrines at Mahabalipuram, though some sources describe the style as early Chalukyan, and the patron dynasty is not firmly established. The site was formerly in Prakasam district and now falls in the new Markapuram district.
significance: Pilgrims visit the cave shrines, the Durga (Trimukha Durga) temple and the waterfall that drops nearby. On Karthika Pournami (October-November) moonlight is said to fall on the image of the goddess, and the day draws large crowds; Maha Shivaratri is also celebrated. The site is also popular for its forest setting.

pujas.name: Karthika Pournami
pujas.description: Full-moon festival when moonlight is said to fall on the goddess's image.

pujas.name: Maha Shivaratri
pujas.description: Annual Shiva festival at the cave shrines.

name: Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy Temple, Singarayakonda
summary: Hill shrine of Varaha Lakshmi Narasimha at Singarayakonda, about 30 km south of Ongole, with a Prasanna Anjaneya shrine at the foot of the hill.
history: A local legend tells of the demon Kharasura, a devotee of Narasimha who later turned against the sages and was promised his end in the Rama avatar. Accounts of the construction differ: one attributes the hill temple to a Vijayanagara king Devaraya in the 14th-15th century, and an inscription on the Garuda stambham is dated to 1443-44.
significance: The town takes its name from the Narasimha shrine (Singaraya) on the hill. Pilgrims usually visit both the Narasimha temple on the hill and the Prasanna Anjaneya Swamy temple below. Annual festival details could not be confirmed from reliable sources.

name: Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy Temple, Malakonda (Malyadri)
address: Malakonda, Valetivaripalem mandal, on the Kandukur-Pamur road, Prakasam
summary: Hill temple of Malyadri Lakshmi Narasimha near Valetivaripalem, about 34 km from Kandukur, open for darshan only on Saturdays.
history: According to the sthala purana, the sage Agastya did penance on this hill and Narasimha appeared to him as a red flame, so he is called Jwala Narasimha. The hill's name is explained as Vishnu's garland (mala) turned into a hill (adri) by Lakshmi. The district administration notes that the shrine has no documented historical record or notable architecture.
significance: The temple is unusual in that it opens for darshan only on Saturdays, when devotees from Prakasam and Nellore climb the hill. Pilgrims come to pray to Narasimha for protection and to fulfil vows.
